claims.text: Combining in situ high-temperature DSC/synchrotron X-ray diffraction with electromagnetic levitation and laser vibrometry can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties in high-entropy alloys.
The approach can be extended from prototype CoCrFeMnNi to other HEAs, including Al-containing variants.
Heating rates of 1–5 °C/min up to approximately 2000 °C under inert gas or vacuum are suitable operating conditions for the DSC/synchrotron measurements.
Real-time diffraction-peak changes indicate the onset of melting and lattice expansion.
Surface-vibration modes measured during levitation correlate with liquid density and volume changes.
DSC heat-flow profiles quantify the enthalpy of fusion.
Disappearance of crystalline diffraction peaks in conjunction with DSC marks the melting temperature.
The combined melting temperature and fusion enthalpy measurements enable extraction of the entropy of fusion.
Containerless electromagnetic levitation minimizes heterogeneous and container-induced effects during melting.
Laser-vibrometry frequency shifts are directly linked to changes in liquid density and volume.
Correlating thermal, diffraction, and vibration signals provides cross-validation of thermodynamic transitions and liquid-phase properties.
The integrated method can determine melting temperatures within ±2–3 °C.
The integrated method can determine latent heat within ±5%.
The combined diffraction and vibrometry signals can reliably measure volume change at melting and liquid-density variations.
The stated performance is applicable across a broad range of high-configurational-entropy alloy compositions.
Conventional DSC and other single-method approaches can suffer from container-induced artifacts and limited structural resolution.
The approach is best suited to electrically conductive high-entropy metallic alloys.
Highly reactive compositions or compositions with unusual magnetic behavior may require additional calibration.
The absolute calibration between vibrational frequency and liquid density may depend on HEA composition.
Quantitative performance across the full HEA compositional landscape has not been verified.
